On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya is the dominant figure: he confronts Sitaram, and Sitaram submits, asking to be disarmed and bound. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, the dynamic reverses: Sitaram takes charge, grabs Udayaditya, and physically carries him out of prison, leaving Udayaditya passive and dependent.

Pratapaditya’s initial failed plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; the Pathan who met him on the road did not kill him. The method that finally succeeded was a signed execution order sent through Muktiyar Khan to Raigarh, where Basanta Ray was killed with a sword by Abdul.
In the Mahishi’s room in the inner quarters, while disguised as a middle-aged woman; and in the king’s room, while unmasked as Ramai Bhand, the jester.
The covert poisoning of Surma—Mangala’s prepared poisoned medicine—caused her death, ending her stay rather than an ordinary exile.
Ramchandra Ray takes revenge by taking another wife, so when Vibha finally comes, it is too late for her to be part of the marriage.

Udayaditya gives his ring to Rukmini, and the ring’s seal is used to forge and stamp a false petition in his name accusing him of treason against Pratapaditya; Bhagavat delivers that petition to Pratapaditya, and it is used as the reason for imprisoning Udayaditya.

Ramchandra Ray’s escape led to the dismissal of the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat; Udayaditya and then Surma secretly gave them stipends, and Pratapaditya’s discovery of those secret stipends led him to order Surma to be sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses profound loneliness, loss, and emptiness: those Basanta Ray loved are absent, no one answers his call, and his singing has lost its earlier joy. He sings it first in a private, reflective moment on the veranda of his Raigarh palace at sunset, and again in the dark, silent household of Jessore, taking Vibha’s hand after seeing the empty room and learning that Udayaditya is in prison.

Her failure let Udayaditya escape to Raigarh with Basanta Ray; Pratapaditya, informed of the escape and Rukmini’s accusation that the old king had helped, ordered the King of Raigarh killed, and Muktiyar Khan executed Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya’s initial reception of Ramchandra Ray was curt, sparse, and almost deliberately unceremonious—he gave no royal fanfare, no proper welcome at first, and only a small, delayed escort—which Ramchandra took as a grave insult. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra addressed Pratapaditya’s status by openly belittling him, mocking his lineage and dynasty, asserting his own superiority, and letting courtiers daily tear Pratapaditya’s reputation to shreds.

By leaving Raigarh and living on the outskirts of Jessore as “Mangala,” befriends palace servants, uses tantric poison and the Rajmahishi’s hostility toward Surma to cause Surma to die, and then appears to Udayaditya demanding his love and ring.

His early rejection of being crown prince and heir hardens into formal renunciation when he is brought before Pratapaditya and declares he does not want Jessore’s throne; to prove the truth of his heart, he swears before Ma-Kali that he will never rule even a needle’s tip of Jessore, never sit on its throne or touch its scepter, and that Samaraditya shall be heir, after which Pratapaditya agrees and Udayaditya leaves the kingdom.

The letter meant for Pratapaditya is handed to the Mahishi by the old Nayanchand, who fears delivering it; the Mahishi keeps it secret and shows it only to Basanta Ray, who then tells Vibha and the household that Ramchandra Ray wrote a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip, so Vibha believes he is calling her rather than rejecting her.

Pratapaditya’s trap fails because he blocks the canal with large sal-wood logs, but when Ramchandra Ray’s boat is stopped there, Rammohan and his men pull it up and over the logs, and the delayed and ineffective guard response lets them escape to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray’s sitar symbolizes the joy and companionship of his family life; when he leaves it behind and says he will not play it again, and later finds it absent, its strings broken and it untunable, his music becomes empty and sorrowful. This reflects his deepening despair over Udayaditya’s separation and imprisonment, as the loss of his beloved sitar mirrors the loss of his loved ones and the emptiness left behind.

Earlier, Udayaditya was willing to intervene boldly against oppression and protect his subjects without regard for consequences. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitant and ineffective: he no longer stops officials or helps the oppressed, and even when a subject is beaten, he runs away instead of acting.
He rescues Udayaditya from prison by telling him the prison is on fire and leading him out to safety during the fire.

He carries them out physically: first he lowers Maharaj Ramchandra Ray, tied to his back, down a rope made of sheets and drops him into a boat; second, he lifts the fainted princess Vibha, brings her out of the palace, and places her in a palanquin for the boat.

At Jessore she is lavishly and heavily adorned in her mother-in-law’s fashion—eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, an elaborate coiffure, and a joy-flushed face—whereas at Chandradwip she comes in plain commoner’s or beggar-woman dress, unadorned and veiled, entering the palace like a maidservant rather than a queen.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window symbolizes memory, absence, and longing—it is the place where Surma used to sit, now empty, while Udayaditya watches for her. In the prison cell, the window becomes a symbol of freedom and hope: looking through it at the sky and birds makes Udayaditya feel that his cage may break and that, even in imprisonment, he can still imagine liberation.

Sitaram, a penniless guard, uses flirtation, false excuses, and witty banter to borrow from Rukmini, and their repeated visits and secret conferences turn the money-lending arrangement into a conspiratorial relationship. It becomes life-threatening when Sitaram, after participating in the fire and making the Yubaraj’s death seem certain, goes to Rukmini’s dark cottage at night to steal her money; there he finds her furious and delirious, she threatens to kill him and the Yubaraj, seizes a curved blade, and forces Sitaram to flee for his life.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire only as a distraction: the noise and panic make the guards near Udayaditya’s prison run away, allowing Sitaram to grab Udayaditya and take him out. He then turns the fire into a full cover-up by, with accomplices, spreading it so it cannot be put out, setting Udayaditya’s empty prison cell ablaze, and staging signs of his death—screams heard from inside, a collapsed roof, and an inaccessible burning cell. He plants bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword in the cell, and the resulting rumors and “evidence” make the palace believe Udayaditya died in the fire, masking his escape.

He interprets Udayaditya’s protective act as expected and not selfless, believing Udayaditya mainly saved him for the sake of his own sister, so he shows no gratitude and instead ridicules him in court.

By forging a petition in the Yubaraj’s seal and presenting it to Pratapaditya as if Udayaditya had lodged a treasonous complaint with the Emperor of Delhi, Bhagavat turns the emperor’s feared authority into a pretext for imprisoning the prince.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair marks Surma’s presence because Surma is the one who braids and styles Vibha’s hair and tends to her personally. After Surma’s disappearance, Vibha waits at the usual hair-braiding time expecting Surma to come, but she does not, and Vibha’s hair remains unbraided and unkempt, making Surma’s tragic absence visibly present in the Jessore palace.
